title: CRINK: the coalition that isn’t
author: Khang Vu
text: Defence & security, explained.Partners forever, but everywhere? (Alexander Kazakov via Getty Images)CRINK: the coalition that isn’tGrouping four different threats under one acronym flatters Washington’s rivals with a unity they don’t have.Khang Vu4 September 20264 min read|CRINK: the coalition that isn’tCRINK: the coalition that isn’tRussian President Vladimir Putin’s visit (Opens in new window) to the Russian-controlled disputed Iturup of the southern Kuril Islands, North Korea’s short-range ballistic missile tests (Opens in new window) over the Sea of Japan and China’s condemnations (Opens in new window) of Japan’s statement on possible involvement in a Taiwan contingency together leave the impression (Opens in new window) of a revisionist China-Russia-North Korea bloc jointly challenging the US-led order.Some Western officials and think tanks have (Opens in new window) dubbed (Opens in new window) the bloc – Iran included – as CRINK. The 2026 US National Defence Strategy (Opens in new window) explicitly names the four CRINK countries as a threat and assumes they can coordinate attacks across multiple theatres simultaneously.But there is a danger in treating CRINK as a revisionist (Opens in new window) cohesive bloc.China and North Korea would rather profit from Russia’s and Iran’s wars instead of fighting their own against the West.The acronym falsely attributes aggressive intentions to all its members and demands that the United States be everywhere all at once. China and North Korea are (Opens in new window) indeed helping (Opens in new window) Iran and Russia fight (Opens in new window) against the United States and Ukraine, but that does not mean they will themselves launch an invasion of Taiwan or South Korea, respectively.Russia and North Korea revived a Cold War-era alliance treaty in June 2024 and promised military aid if either is under attack. Pyongyang has sent approximately 16,000 troops (Opens in new window) to help Russia defend Kursk (Opens in new window) from Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s possible help with missile (Opens in new window) and submarine (Opens in new window) technologies.In January 2025, Russia signed (Opens in new window) a non-aggression pact with Iran and have been (Opens in new window) providing (Opens in new window) intelligence, drones, and missiles to Tehran to target US warships and aircraft in the Middle East. North Korea is suspected (Opens in new window) of supplying weapons to Iran-backed Hamas to fight Israel. Both countries can expand (Opens in new window) their missile cooperation by sharing data on the performances of North Korean missile in Ukraine and Iranian missiles in the Middle East.China maintains (Opens in new window) a mutual defence pact with North Korea, it affirms (Opens in new window) a no limits partnership with Russia, and it is accused (Opens in new window) by the West of supplying shoulder-fired anti-air missile systems to Iran.The West has sought to weaken CRINK via sanctions and multi-theatre military deterrence. Washington imposed (Opens in new window) sanctions (Opens in new window) on North Korean and Chinese entities who are involved in facilitating financial and military assistance to Russia. It also broadens (Opens in new window) secondary sanctions on countries (Opens in new window) trading with Iran. NATO has prepared (Opens in new window) itself for possible Iranian attacks against US bases across Europe. It launched (Opens in new window) the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List to coordinate and fund weapons supplies to Ukraine and has counted non-NATO Australia (Opens in new window), New Zealand (Opens in new window), and Japan (Opens in new window) among the contributors.China and North Korea differ with Russia and Iran over the status quo of the US-led order in their respective neighbourhoods (Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images)Washington has also urged (Opens in new window) South Korea and Japan to contribute ships to reopen the Strait of Hormuz although the US–South Korea (Opens in new window) and US–Japan alliance (Opens in new window) treaties do not cover the Middle East. The United States wants its European (Opens in new window) and Asian (Opens in new window) allies to increase spending on core military priorities to 3.5% of GDP to contain CRINK on multiple fronts.However, there are big differences between CRINK countries that undermine the assumption of simultaneity behind the acronym.China and North Korea differ with Russia and Iran over the status quo of the US-led order in their respective neighbourhoods. Russia launched (Opens in new window) the war against Ukraine as a response to perceptions of Kyiv moving closer to NATO. Iran attacks US bases in the Middle East to permanently weaken (Opens in new window) its neighbours’ will to host the US military and degrade (Opens in new window) Washington’s capability to launch air strikes.China has shown (Opens in new window) concern (Opens in new window) about growing US-led coordination among Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and the Philippines, but its response is short of outright military action (Opens in new window). China has rejected (Opens in new window) any accusations of an imminent invasion of Taiwan and US intelligence agrees (Opens in new window) with this assessment.North Korea likewise condemns (Opens in new window) US “hostile policy,” but it rejects allegations (Opens in new window) of invading the South by recognising (Opens in new window) it as a separate state in the recent constitutional revision. And if simultaneity holds, China and North Korea should have mobilised for wars against Taiwan and South Korea as Russia (Opens in new window) and Iran (Opens in new window) counterattacked against Ukraine and the United States.The uncertain outcome of Russia’s and Iran’s wars cautions China and North Korea against military adventurism. For China, the two wars show the limit of a great power’s ability to subdue a smaller enemy, as ballistic missiles and drones allow (Opens in new window) the weaker to overwhelm air-defence systems and disrupt (Opens in new window) troops movement of the stronger. North Korea, which has invested more in deterring an invasion than launching one, is grasping the limits (Opens in new window) of its conventional arsenal (Opens in new window) in fighting a ground and a naval war. Russia being occupied with Ukraine and China’s rejection (Opens in new window) of military aid were North Korea to attack the South first only strengthens Pyongyang’s restraint.A defence strategy based on an assumption of simultaneity behind CRINK will weaken US deterrence. Preparing to fight in multiple theatres at once requires extension of deployment for military platforms at the expense (Opens in new window) of morale and maintenance. The United States doesn’t have (Opens in new window) enough missile interceptors to contain CRINK in Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific. Once Washington faces the inevitability of prioritising (Opens in new window) one theatre over another, its pledge to defend allies will be subject to extreme scrutiny.A simple acronym cannot capture the diverse priorities and threat perceptions of each CRINK state. Russia and Iran do not want to be entrapped in a Pacific war, while China and North Korea would rather profit from Russia’s and Iran’s wars instead of fighting their own against the West.About the authorKhang VuKhang Vu is a visiting scholar in the Political Science Department at Boston College.TopicsDefence & securityChinaRussiaIranNorth KoreaUnited StatesThe Interpreter on Defence & securityExplore The InterpreterGender & equalityBeyond the count: the killing of Indigenous women as a security crisis2 September 2026Kyllie Cripps ,Sara E DaviesJapanSanae Takaichi’s strong poll position masks a brittle mandate1 September 2026Ryosuke HanadaUkraineThe US Army lost against Ukraine but would Australia do any better?28 August 2026Mick RyanMore on Defence & securityExplore Defence & securityConversationsPacific unity on the line: The 2026 PIF Leaders' MeetingOliver Nobetau, Connor Graham, Sarah ThompsonResearchFault lines beneath the Blue Pacific: Deep-sea mining and the future of Pacific unityAnalysis by Connor GrahamEvent ReplayLowy Institute debate: Does AUKUS strengthen Australia's security?Sam Roggeveen, Jennifer Parker, Mihai SoraEvent ReplayPrime Minister of Thailand Anutin CharnvirakulAnutin Charnvirakul, Michael Fullilove
